title: A predictive microscopic theory of cuprate superconductivity

concept.text: Discovered Materials grand challenge 01: explain how superconductivity arises from the cuprates' unusual normal state, and predict their phase diagram from a microscopic theory. Sources given: https://discoveredmaterials.com/grand-challenges/.

change_log.change: Added by hand to PHY on 2026-11-15.
change_log.reason: Grand challenge published by Discovered Materials (Matforge Inc.), open as of November 2026 with a USD 1 million prize pool; added at the owner's request, November 14, 2026.

page.title: A predictive microscopic theory of cuprate superconductivity
page.definition: A theory starting from electron and atomic interactions explains superconductivity—zero resistance and magnetic-flux expulsion—in cuprates, layered copper oxides. It predicts their phase diagram, the phases present versus temperature and carrier concentration, and explains the conducting state above the transition.

goal.need: Choosing which cuprates to make still depends heavily on trial and error. Linking composition and crystal structure to transition temperature would let materials developers select candidates for synthesis. Warmer operation could also reduce the cost of cooling power cables. At the AmpaCity installation in Essen, an estimated 43 kW of electrical power supplied 3.4 kW of cooling, including the energy for nitrogen liquefaction and transport. A new conductor would have to carry the required current at the higher temperature.

completion.title: Discovered Materials judges a microscopic theory to satisfy every criterion of its cuprate challenge.
completion.criterion: Discovered Materials accepts a reproducible microscopic theory under Challenge 01. Its 12 benchmarks cover the phase diagram; gap symmetry and magnitude; pseudogap spectra; resistivity; specific heat and entropy; superfluid density; antiferromagnetism; magnetic excitations; charge order; elastic and symmetry-breaking responses; and local pairing. These must follow quantitatively from a physically justified Hamiltonian, the equation specifying the system’s energy, without fitting each observable independently. Calibration observations must be distinguished from independent predictions.
completion.set_by: Discovered Materials, Grand Challenges Official Rules, sections 4–5, incorporating the Challenge 01 description.
completion.threshold_quote: A challenge is "solved" only when a submission meets every success criterion in its Challenge Description
completion.basis: The decision belongs to the prize sponsor. It assesses accuracy, breadth, physical consistency, novelty and reproducibility. It publishes no numerical error tolerances. If the sponsor requests verification, the submission is disqualified if the result cannot be verified or reproduced within 90 days of the request. The sponsor listed Challenge 01 as open in November 2026.

milestones.title: A cuprate exhibits half-quantum flux in a phase-sensitive test of d-wave pairing.
milestones.criterion: Measure spontaneous magnetic flux of h/(4e), half the superconducting flux quantum, in a cuprate ring whose junction orientations frustrate a d-wave order parameter. Check that otherwise comparable unfrustrated rings lack the spontaneous half quantum. Here h is Planck’s constant and e is the elementary charge.
milestones.set_by: The phase-sensitive pairing-symmetry convention reviewed by Tsuei and Kirtley; the cited initial demonstration used YBa₂Cu₃O₇−δ.
milestones.threshold_quote: the half-integer flux-quantum effect as an unambiguous signature

milestones.title: A theory predicts local pair-density changes from charge-transfer energy.
milestones.criterion: For a specified cuprate and doping, predict the sign and magnitude of the local change in superconducting pair density with the energy required to transfer charge between oxygen and copper. Compare with spatially resolved measurements using the same pair-density normalization. State whether, in the theory, magnetic exchange mediated by virtual charge transfer drives pairing.
milestones.threshold_quote: whether charge-transfer superexchange sets the pairing

milestones.title: A theory predicts the cuprate pseudogap energy and electron spectrum versus temperature and doping.
milestones.criterion: Predict the single-electron spectral function A(k, ω), which resolves electronic spectral weight by momentum and energy, and the energy scale of the pseudogap. Compare their evolution with temperature and doping against spectra from underdoped cuprates, including the depletion of low-energy weight above the superconducting transition.

milestones.title: A theory predicts the magnitude of in-plane cuprate resistivity versus temperature and doping.
milestones.criterion: Calculate the normal-state electrical resistivity within the copper–oxygen planes for a specified cuprate. Compare its absolute magnitude, its variation with temperature and the change of that temperature dependence with doping against transport measurements.

milestones.title: A theory predicts superconducting domes across cuprate material families.
milestones.criterion: For each cuprate family studied, calculate the bulk superconducting transition temperature as a function of hole concentration per planar copper atom. Compare both ends of the superconducting doping range, the doping at the maximum and the maximum temperature with experiment. Use the same microscopic framework to account for differences in dome shape and height across families.
milestones.set_by: Discovered Materials, Challenge 01, benchmark 1 and its cross-family phase-diagram comparison.

milestones.title: A resistive transition and magnetic flux expulsion establish superconductivity in a cuprate.
milestones.criterion: Measure the drop in resistivity on cooling and the diamagnetic response associated with expulsion of magnetic flux. In a specimen containing several crystalline phases, identify which cuprate phase carries the superconductivity.
milestones.set_by: The experimental convention applied by Bednorz and Müller in identifying superconductivity in barium-doped lanthanum cuprate.
milestones.threshold_quote: The final proof of superconductivity, the presence of the Meissner-Ochsenfeld effect

milestones.title: A theory predicts the cuprate superconducting gap magnitude across momentum, temperature and doping.
milestones.criterion: Calculate the magnitude of the superconducting energy gap as a function of electron momentum, temperature and doping for a specified cuprate. Compare the predicted energy scale and momentum dependence with measurements from angle-resolved photoemission and scanning tunneling microscopy.

milestones.title: A theory predicts the energies, widths and spectral weights of cuprate magnetic excitations.
milestones.criterion: Calculate the dynamical spin structure factor, which gives the strength of spin fluctuations at each transferred momentum and energy. Compare predicted excitation energies, linewidths and spectral weights across doping with neutron scattering or resonant inelastic X-ray scattering measurements.

milestones.title: One microscopic theory supplies reproducible predictions for all 12 cuprate benchmarks.
milestones.criterion: Provide the predictions for all 12 experimental targets from one physically justified Hamiltonian. Identify which observations fixed its parameters and which were predicted independently. Supply a technical account sufficient to repeat the calculations, with supporting data and, for computational results, the code, inputs and parameter values.
milestones.set_by: Discovered Materials, Challenge 01 submission requirements and Official Rules, section 4.
milestones.threshold_quote: with the code, inputs and parameters used

not_found: No numerical acceptance tolerances, prescribed doping grid or minimum family count were found in the challenge description or official rules.

results.finding: The LSCO-like Emery model, sampled at five hole concentrations, predicts a normal-state pseudogap over δn = 0.05–0.15 at the lowest temperature studied.
results.detail: The pseudogap range is compared with ARPES and Nernst measurements near 100 K. The momentum-resolved calculations shown are at 251.33 and 377 K.

results.finding: The LSCO-like Emery model, sampled at five hole concentrations, predicts incommensurate static spin response starting at δn = 0.15.
results.detail: The susceptibility maps are calculated at 251.33 and 377 K. The authors attribute the earlier experimental onset to neutron measurements at temperatures of about 40 K or lower.

results.finding: One overdoped Bi2212 film reached zero resistance below 50 K.
results.quote:
The superconducting transition temperature Tc =  50 K was determined as 
the temperature below which the zero-field resistance R =  0.

results.finding: For one Bi2212 film, the Planckian estimate of the in-plane sheet-resistivity slope was 7.4 ± 1.4 Ω K⁻¹.
results.detail: The estimate uses the Drude formula and assumes a Planckian scattering rate. High-field measurements suppressed superconductivity in Bi2212. The Bi2201 comparison used previously reported transport data.
results.quote:
the Planckian limit predicts 
A1□ =  7.4 ±  1.4 Ω  K−1, while we measured A 1□ =  8.0 ±  0.9 Ω  K−1

results.finding: Across three La-214 compounds, the Planckian comparison gives a predicted sheet-resistivity slope of 8.9 ± 1.8 Ω K⁻¹ for LSCO.
results.detail: The slope comparison uses transport data at three dopings per compound. Two Nd-LSCO doping points were measured under pressure to suppress the pseudogap.
results.quote:
the Planckian

results.finding: For one LSCO ARPES condition, the Hubbard-model nodal spectrum needed 0.5 eV of added broadening.
results.detail: The direct line-shape comparison uses a single nodal spectrum. The gaps quantified in the doping scans are the Hubbard Mott gap and the Emery charge-transfer gap.

with a phenomenological frequency-independent imag-

results.finding: Across three La-214 compounds, Hubbard-model resistivity agrees with LCCO transport up to about 150 K.
results.detail: Figure 15 compares four LSCO, four LBCO and five LCCO doping levels. The authors choose the Hubbard coupling for best transport agreement and add a temperature-independent residual offset to each curve.

results.detail: The calculation uses doping near the experimental optimum. Uncertainty in apical oxygen position propagates into the inferred temperatures, especially for Bi2201.

results.finding: Across five Hg-based compounds, stronger pairing correlates with a smaller charge-transfer gap, about 0.75 eV in the bilayer parent’s outer plane.
results.detail: The charge-transfer gaps are evaluated in parent compounds, while the order parameters are calculated in hole-doped compounds. The study also finds that layer doping and orbital splitting influence the order parameter.
results.quote:
In the outer
planes of nHBCCO, mSC sharply increases from n ¼ 1 to
n ¼ 2 and then saturates, consistent with the n dependence
of the CTG and J (see Fig. 10).

results.finding: Two Hg-based compounds have doping-resolved spectra. The trilayer shows an antinodal pseudogap at 50% nominal doping.
results.detail: The nominal doping is applied to the charge reservoir. The effective doping of individual CuO₂ planes is lower, and the trilayer planes remain underdoped at this setting.
results.quote:
Finally, at substantial doping ( δtot ¼ 50%), where CuO 2
planes are still underdoped, we identify a spectral weight
transfer above the Fermi level for all planes in both nCCOC
and nHBCCO, with a clear pseudogap feature in the
antinodal region (orange arrows no. 2).

results.finding: Across five Hg-based compounds, the calculated zero-temperature pairing onset is near 4% planar hole doping.
results.detail: The reported experimental comparison is with the onset of a superconducting gap in a six-layer cuprate. In the Hg-based single-layer calculation, effective doping saturates before the overdoped pairing endpoint is reached.
results.quote:
We observe that mSC is always vanishing when the
estimated doping is below about 4%, in remarkable
agreement with the opening of the superconducting gap at
4.3% doping observed with ARPES in the n ¼ 6 multilayer
cuprate [67] and reproduced in Fig. 17(b).

results.finding: Across 3 Hg-cuprate structures, the estimated maximum pairing gap increases from single-layer Hg-1201 to 2-layer oxidized Hg-1212.
results.detail: The paper compares the layer trend with measured transition temperatures using a weak-coupling relation.
results.quote:
The maximum pairing gap Eg (right axis of
Fig. 3D) shows the same behavior as the pairing order.

results.finding: In 2 Hg-1212 structures, the reduced form has weaker computed pairing near nominal total hole doping of 0.5.
results.detail: The two structures differ in charge distribution. Oxygen hole content and bond order serve as descriptors related to charge transfer.
results.quote:
where the effective Cu doping is smaller in
the reduced structure than the oxidized structure, along with
a reduction in pairing order (as in the experiment, but much
larger in magnitude).

results.finding: For 3 Hg-cuprate structures, ground-state pairing curves reproduce the layer trend toward the measured 127 K transition of double-layer Hg-1212.
results.detail: The experimental temperature is a comparison point in Fig. 3. The calculated doping curves track pairing order and an auxiliary gap.
results.quote:
We see a sizable
increase in the maximum pairing order moving from Hg-1201
to Hg-1212 (ox).

results.detail: RIXS linewidths were fitted across doping. The calculated spectra were broadened predominantly by the simulation temperature (T = 0.15 eV).

results.detail: The band parameters were fitted to a bismuth cuprate Fermi surface. The authors adjusted the interaction prefactor at each doping to match the odd-mode energy. The reported narrower even Q* branch refers to its energy range.

results.detail: The authors fit the hopping parameter to the measured slope at δ = 0.15 and 200 K. At each doping they estimate a temperature-independent impurity offset by matching the calculated and measured resistivity at 200 K.
